objectives.text: Define food security and food insecurity, and give the scale of the problem.
Name factors driving food prices and say who they affect.
Say what the food industry covers and weigh processing's benefits against its costs.
Name concrete steps toward a more sustainable food pattern.
Distinguish an evidence-based diet from a fashionable one.
Judge a nutrition claim carried by the media.

terms.gloss: Continual access to safe, sufficient food. Its absence is food insecurity.
Everything from production and manufacturing to distribution, marketing and retail.
Treatment that extends shelf life and improves safety and supply — at some cost to nutrients.
One that can keep feeding people without exhausting what it depends on.
One of several patterns with actual evidence behind it, alongside DASH and vegetarian diets.
An area where affordable, nutritious food is hard to reach — access as a barrier, not knowledge.

options: Continual access to safe, sufficient food
Having enough money to buy any food at all
Growing some of your own food at home
A guaranteed national supply of the staple grains
questions.why: Continual is the operative word. Someone who eats today but cannot count on tomorrow is food insecure.
distractorNotes: Income helps but is not the definition.
National supply does not guarantee household access.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many people worldwide live with constant hunger?
options: Close to one billion
Close to one million
Close to ten thousand
Close to ten billion
questions.why: The figure is on the order of a billion — about one person in eight at the time the chapter was written.
distractorNotes: Three orders of magnitude too low.
More than the world's whole population.

questions.prompt: Which is named as a driver of rising food prices?
options: Population growth and natural disasters
A worldwide fall in the demand for grain crops
Reduced spending on food advertising
Lower fuel costs in food transportation
questions.why: Several forces push at once — more people, disrupted harvests, higher input costs — and they fall hardest on those with least margin.
distractorNotes: Fuel costs rising, not falling, feeds through to price.

questions.prompt: Food processing is best described as:
options: A trade-off between safety and nutrients
An unambiguous harm to public health
A purely commercial decision by industry
A process that always adds more nutrients
questions.why: Processing improves safety, shelf life and supply, and can cost nutrients. Weighing both is the honest position.
distractorNotes: It has real benefits, including safety.
It has public-health consequences either way.
Some processing fortifies; much does not.

questions.prompt: Which is a concrete step toward a sustainable food pattern?
options: Buying locally grown food where you can
Buying only the imported organic produce
Eating nothing but raw uncooked foods
Refusing all commercially sold food
questions.why: The chapter's suggestions are small and cumulative — local sourcing, less waste, seasonal eating — rather than dramatic.
distractorNotes: Importing adds transport cost, sustainable or not.

questions.prompt: Which diets does the chapter name as evidence-based?
options: Mediterranean, DASH and vegetarian
Any diet that eliminates carbohydrate
Whichever diet is currently popular
Only diets prescribed by a physician
questions.why: These have research behind them. The point is to ground choices in fact rather than fashion.
distractorNotes: Popularity is precisely the wrong test.
Evidence is not limited to prescriptions.

questions.prompt: A magazine reports one study showing a food prevents cancer. The right response is:
options: Ask what the whole body of evidence says
Accept it, since a real study was published
Dismiss all reporting about nutrition
Adopt it until another study appears
questions.why: A single study is one data point. Scientific consensus is built over time, and the media reports individual studies as though they were conclusions.
distractorNotes: That is how diet fashions replace each other.

questions.prompt: What does the food industry cover?
options: Production, distribution, marketing, retail
Only the farms that grow raw crops
Only supermarkets and the grocery store chains
Only manufacturers of packaged goods
questions.why: It is the whole chain. Which matters, because a change at any point along it reaches your plate.
distractorNotes: Farming is one link in the chain.

questions.prompt: Family meals and home-cooked food are associated with:
options: Better health and other benefits too
Higher food costs and nothing else
Worse nutrition than eating out does
No measurable difference in outcomes
questions.why: The studies cited find benefits beyond nutrition alone, which is a reason to treat cooking as more than fuel preparation.
distractorNotes: The evidence runs the other way.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter insist on grounding diet in fact rather than fashion?
options: Attitudes to food shift over time
Because all popular diets are harmful
Because science never changes at all
Because fashion is illegal to advertise
questions.why: What is fashionable changes; what is supported changes much more slowly and for different reasons. Knowing which you are following is the skill.

checklist: Pick one food you eat often and trace where it comes from.
Name one factor that would raise its price and say who that hurts most.
Name one change that would make your own pattern more sustainable.
Find one nutrition claim in the media and say what evidence would settle it.
selfCheck: Did I separate a single study from a body of evidence?
Did I treat access and cost as real constraints, not just choices?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
